precepts.text: Whosoever came to the king into the inner court uncalled would be put to death, except the king held out the golden sceptre.
precepts.point: Then God changed the spirit of the king into mildness. He leaped from his throne, took her in his arms until she came to herself, and comforted her with loving words. The Most High turned the king's heart.
precepts.why:
Her “countenance was cheerful and very amiable: but her heart was in anguish for fear”, and the fear had a reason. Esther herself had said it: “whosoever, whether man or woman, shall come unto the king into the inner court, who is not called, there is one law of his to put him to death, except such to whom the king shall hold out the golden sceptre, that he may live: but I have not been called to come in unto the king these thirty days.”

The only time anyone could come before the king was when called, and she had not been called in thirty days. She was coming without going through the proper order, with one law standing against her. So when the king, “very dreadful” in his robes of majesty, “looked very fiercely upon her”, the queen “fell down, and was pale, and fainted”. She was looking at the law of death, with only the golden sceptre between her and it.

precepts.text: The king's heart is in the hand of the Lord, and he turneth it whithersoever he will.
precepts.point: Then God changed the spirit of the king into mildness. He leaped from his throne, took her in his arms until she came to herself, and comforted her with loving words. The Most High turned the king's heart.
precepts.why:
The king looked very fiercely upon her and she fainted; then God changed the spirit of the king into mildness. He leaped from his throne, took her in his arms until she came to herself, and comforted her with loving words.

“The king’s heart is in the hand of the Lord, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will.” That is what happened between the fierce look and the loving words. The Most High turned the king's heart. The one law was to put her to death, and the king was very dreadful, but his heart was not his own to keep hard; it is in the hand of the Lord, and he turned it for Esther and for his people.

points: Upon the third day, when she had ended her prayer, Esther laid away her mourning garments and put on her glorious apparel. The prayer came first; the appearance before the king came after.

Being gloriously adorned, she first called upon God, who is the beholder and saviour of all things, and then took two maids with her. She leaned upon one, carrying herself daintily, while the other bore up her train.

Esther was ruddy through the perfection of her beauty, her countenance cheerful and amiable, but her heart was in anguish for fear. The only time one could come before the king was when called, and she was coming without going through the proper order.

She passed through all the doors and stood before the king, who sat upon his royal throne clothed with robes of majesty glittering with gold and precious stones, and he was very dreadful. When he lifted up his countenance and looked fiercely upon her, the queen fainted and bowed herself upon the head of her maid.

Then God changed the spirit of the king into mildness. He leaped from his throne, took her in his arms until she came to herself, and comforted her with loving words. The Most High turned the king's heart.

Not only did the Most High change the spirit of the king when Esther came in, but he had changed it altogether. The king who was so easily persuaded by Haman at first was now moved by the Most High to be persuaded by Esther.

The king said unto Esther, I am thy brother, be of good cheer; thou shalt not die, though our commandment be general. Though the law was that none uncalled should live, the king made her the exception. He held up his golden sceptre and laid it upon her neck and embraced her.

Esther told the king she saw him as an angel of God, and her heart was troubled for fear of his majesty, calling him wonderful and his countenance full of grace. As she was speaking she fell down for faintness.
The king was troubled and all his servants comforted her. The whole scene shows how the Most High had prepared the way and turned the king toward mercy before a single request was even made.
